title: Gilgamesh: the first hero of history
subtitle: Mesopotamia
subject: mythologie
description: King of Uruk, friend of Enkidu, seeker of immortality: the Epic of Gilgamesh, written 4,000 years ago, is the oldest great story of humanity.

hero.hook: Before Homer, before the Bible: a king terrified of death sets off to the ends of the earth... and brings back a lesson, not eternity.

blocks.text: **Gilgamesh**, king of the city of **Uruk** in Mesopotamia, is the hero of the **Epic of Gilgamesh**. Engraved on clay tablets more than **4,000 years ago**, this work predates Homer and the biblical stories.
It's not just an adventure. It's the story of a tyrant who discovers friendship, then the fear of dying, then a harsh wisdom: immortality is not in the body, but in what we leave behind.

sections.title: An epic out of the sand

blocks.text: The text assembles ancient Sumerian stories. Its classic version, in Akkadian, is attributed to the scribe  (around the 12th century BC). Forgotten under the sands, it resurfaced in the 19th century in the library of the king  in **Nineveh**. [[Sîn-lēqi-unninni]] [[Assurbanipal]]

blocks.caption: Cuneiform tablet from the epic, British Museum.

blocks.text: In **1872**, the Assyriologist **George Smith** deciphered at the British Museum a story of flood, ark and survival, predating Genesis by about a millennium. The writing **cuneiform**, pressed into the clay, saved the text where the papyrus would have disappeared.
Reading the Flood Tablet, George Smith was said to have been so excited that he began to undress in front of his astonished colleagues at the British Museum.

At the beginning, **Gilgamesh** is an insufferable king: two thirds divine, one third human, but tyrant for Uruk. To channel him, the goddess  shapes **Enkidu**, a wild man who lives among gazelles. [[Aruru]]

blocks.caption: Gilgamesh and Enkidu: from fighting to brotherly friendship.

blocks.text: They fight, no one wins, and the rivalry becomes friendship. Together, they kill the monster **Humbaba** in the Cedar Forest, then the **Celestial Bull** sent by the goddess **Ishtar**. The gods, irritated, condemn Enkidu to die of illness. The death of the friend changes everything.

In front of Enkidu's corpse, Gilgamesh understands that he will die too. He abandons his crown, covers himself with animal skins and goes to look for **Ut-napishti**, the only man who became immortal after . The journey takes him beyond the mountains of  and the Waters of Death. [[Account of the Flood in the Epic]] [[Mashu]]

blocks.caption: The story of the Flood: a thousand years before Noah, already on clay.

blocks.text: Ut-napishti imposes a test on him: to stay awake six days and seven nights. Gilgamesh immediately falls asleep. He who does not conquer sleep will not conquer death. He is shown a plant of youth; a snake steals it from him while he is bathing. The snake molts. The king leaves empty-handed.
This  precedes the biblical story of Noah by approximately **1,000 years**: same Mesopotamian cultural background, older version. [[Account of the Flood in the Epic]]

sections.title: The eternity of the walls of Uruk

blocks.text: Back in **Uruk**, Gilgamesh looks at the ramparts of his city. The lesson is clear: biological immortality belongs to the gods. Man endures through his works and through the memory of the living.

Four millennia later, the story still nourishes world culture, from the biblical Noah to the monomyth theories of . To read Gilgamesh is to hear the first great human questions in the face of death. [[Joseph Campbell]]

The **Epic of Gilgamesh**, **4,000 years old**, already contains a flood before the Bible. His hero learns that immortality is not biological: it is in the walls we build and in the memory we leave behind.
